pages.text:
Saturday twenty-nine began with a plan that looked like a spreadsheet from a corporate retreat, if corporate retreats involved stopping time. I had a notebook. I had two columns: PROBLEM and FIX. The first entry was the toast.

At 7:20, I walked into the kitchen and yanked the toaster plug out of the wall before Dad could touch it. He stood there, holding a slice of bread, looking like I had just kicked him in the shin.

"The toaster," he said, "is a democracy."

"I know," I said. "But I'm running for office."

He shrugged, a big, round motion that shook his apron. He walked to the oven, cranked the broiler to red-hot, and shoved the bread in. The smoke alarm screamed thirty seconds later. Dad fanned the ceiling with a dish towel, his mustache twitching.

"Max," he shouted over the beeping. "Did you know that smoke is just air that has given up?"

I wrote in my notebook: PUN: UNSTOPPABLE.

The toast was black. I ate it. It tasted like regret, but the schedule held for one minute, which was more than I had expected from a Saturday.
pages.image: Dad, a large man with a dark mustache and a fish apron, stands in a kitchen fanning a beeping smoke alarm with a dish towel while Max, an 11-year-old in a red hoodie, watches with a scowl from the doorway.

pages.text:
By Saturday thirty, I had learned that preventing bad things was significantly harder than causing them.

At 9:15, the FRAGILE/KITCHEN box sat on the counter like a trap. I grabbed it and carried it to the truck with the intense focus of a surgeon. I placed it gently in the back. It did not drop. I felt a surge of pride so strong it nearly made me dizzy.

Then I sneezed.

The box slipped, hit the pavement, and shattered into a thousand pieces of glass and ceramic. Mom was there, scooping up shards, exactly as usual. I wanted to scream, but I just watched her work.

I tried the sprinkler next. At 4:05, I rushed to the Grady lawn and turned the tap off. The water stopped. Silence. Then, from the side yard, I heard a splash. Mr. Grady had turned his other sprinkler on early. The mailman slipped on a puddle, fell, and his hat flew into a tree.

I sat on the porch steps, my notebook open. The pencil was dull. The world was a whack-a-mole game and I was the mole holding the mallet.
pages.image: Max sits on a porch step holding a notebook, looking defeated, while a mailman in a hat looks up at a tree where his hat is stuck; a sprinkler sprays water in the background.

pages.text:
Saturdays thirty-seven through forty-four turned into a blur of laminated failure. Jonah and I built a spreadsheet. We had four backup plans for Putt-Putt Palace, three for Scoops, and one for the bike chain. It never worked. A bee chased Jonah’s helmet. The bike chain snapped in a way that made a sound like a sad trombone. Scoops ran out of the flavor Jonah loved, which was the color of a bruise.

Each time, we reset. And each time, Jonah looked at me with that huge grin, ready to believe.

"Tell me," he said on Saturday forty-two. "Tell me it’s real."

I was tired. I was so tired of explaining the rules of a game that wasn’t real.

"Go away, Jonah," I snapped.

His face fell. The grin cracked. He turned his bike around and left. I stood there, holding a granola bar, feeling smaller than the bee.
pages.image: Jonah, a tall boy in a bike helmet, looks hurt and turns his bicycle away from Max, who stands with a granola bar in his hand, looking guilty; a parking lot with ice cream cones in the background.

pages.text:
Saturday forty-five was the number that didn't work. I counted the tally marks on the closet wall, one by one, until I reached forty-four, and the numbers sounded flat, like coins dropped on a tile floor. I didn't like that sound.

Then I heard Gus crying.

He was in the hallway. His T. rex tail was caught in the door, and he was pulling at it, but the spikes were hooked on the frame.

"Max!" he wailed.

I ran over. I worked the door open until the tail popped free. Gus stood there, breathing hard, his dinosaur hood askew.

"Thanks," he said.

"You're welcome," I said.

For six minutes, I felt good. I felt useful, like the big brother who actually does things. I stood in the middle of the hall, hands on my hips, breathing deep, because I had fixed it and I had made a difference.

Then the clock ticked.
pages.image: Max helps Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, untangle a spiky tail from a door frame; Max looks focused, Gus looks relieved, morning light streams through the hallway window.

pages.text:
Then Gus reappeared.

Not in the hall, and not six minutes later.

At 6:47 the next morning, the dinosaur climbed onto my chest and screamed.

"RAAAAWR."

I lay flat in the dark, staring at the ceiling while the room remained bare and the box stayed in its place, ready for the day to start all over again.

"You're welcome," I said to the dinosaur.

Gus blinked. He didn't know what I meant. He never did.

I sat up and looked at my hands, realizing that I had fixed the tail, stopped the sprinkler, and eaten the black toast, yet here we were.

It occurred to me that I had done a lot of fixing, and I still hadn't noticed a single thing about anyone but myself.

I looked at the closet wall. Forty-four marks waited there for the forty-fifth.
pages.image: Max sits up in his bare bed, looking thoughtful and a bit lost, while Gus in a T. rex costume sits on his knees; the room is empty except for a cardboard box, grey morning light.
